items.title: L6: One story, several Behaviours
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Most real stories show more than one Behaviour, and assessors score the Behaviour they asked about, so you need to judge which one a story shows best. A useful test is to ask what problem the person was solving and what they personally did about it. Take Priya, who noticed that several letters a week came back marked 'not known at this address'. She compared the records with the latest customer contacts, phoned twenty customers to confirm their details and set up a monthly check so that out-of-date addresses were caught early. Her main Behaviour is Managing a Quality Service, because the story is about accurate records and reliable service for customers. Phoning customers also shows Communicating and Influencing, and the monthly check shows Changing and Improving, but these support the story rather than lead it. If the question was about Changing and Improving, Priya could use the same facts but spend most of the Action on how she spotted the pattern, proposed the check and got it agreed. The facts stay the same; the emphasis changes. Do not try to cover three Behaviours in one 250-word answer. A focused answer on one Behaviour usually scores better than a crowded one that touches several lightly. Choose the story where the Behaviour in the question is the main thing you did.

questions.prompt: Which Behaviour is the main one in Priya's story?

options.text: Managing a Quality Service
Seeing the Big Picture
Delivering at Pace
Working Together

questions.hint: The story is about accurate records and reliable service.

questions.prompt: Which part of Priya's story is the best evidence of Changing and Improving?

options.text: Phoning twenty customers one by one to confirm that their contact details were correct
Setting up a monthly check so out-of-date addresses are caught early
Comparing the records with the most recent customer contacts
Noticing letters coming back marked 'not known at this address'

questions.hint: A new way of working that prevents the problem is the improvement.

questions.prompt: Priya is asked a Changing and Improving question. How should she adapt her answer?

options.text: Choose a completely different story, because a Quality Service story cannot be used to show improvement at any grade
Leave the answer unchanged, because accurate records already cover every Behaviour
Add a short paragraph on each other Behaviour so that nothing is missed
Keep the same facts, but spend most of the Action on spotting and proposing the check

questions.hint: Emphasis shifts to match the Behaviour asked about.

questions.prompt: A 250-word answer touches Leadership, Working Together and Delivering at Pace lightly. Why is it likely to score poorly?

options.text: Assessors mark down any answer that names more than one Behaviour at all
None of the three gets enough specific Action to be properly evidenced
Leadership cannot be shown in a short answer written at entry level
The three Behaviours contradict one another when they appear together

questions.hint: Depth on the Behaviour asked beats a light touch on several.

questions.prompt: Which question helps most when deciding the main Behaviour in a story?

options.text: Which Behaviour name appears first in the list in the advert?
Which part of the story took the longest time to happen?
Which Behaviour do I feel most comfortable talking about?
What problem was being solved, and what did I do about it?

questions.hint: Purpose and personal action reveal the main Behaviour.

questions.prompt: Why does Priya's phoning of customers count as supporting rather than leading evidence?

options.text: Phone calls can never be used to evidence Communicating and Influencing, because assessors only score written work
Only written actions, such as letters and forms, are marked by assessors
It served the aim of accurate records, which is the main point of the story
It happened after the real work was finished, so it cannot be counted

questions.hint: The purpose of the story decides what leads.

questions.prompt: A candidate asked about Working Together describes clearing a backlog alone over a weekend. What is the best advice?

options.text: Add the word 'team' to each sentence so the story sounds collaborative
Keep the story but use 'we' throughout, so that it reads as shared work and sounds collaborative to the assessor
Keep it, because hard work is at the heart of every single Behaviour
Pick a story where cooperation with others is the core of what happened

questions.hint: The evidence must match the Behaviour asked about.

questions.prompt: Assessors scoring an answer to a Behaviour question mainly look for evidence of what?

options.text: Whichever Behaviour the story happens to show best, even if it was not asked
The Behaviour asked about, shown through what the candidate did
A balanced overall picture across all nine of the Behaviours together
The Behaviour that best matches the title of the advertised job

questions.hint: Scoring is against the Behaviour in the question.

questions.prompt: Which detail would most strengthen the Result in Priya's answer?

options.text: A sentence saying that she is a meticulous, careful person who dislikes errors in records
The number of returned letters before and after the monthly check
The name of her line manager
A longer description of the records system

questions.hint: Measured change is stronger than self-description.

questions.prompt: Two helpers in a community group argue over shifts. A volunteer listens to both, brokers a swap that suits each and keeps the rota full. Which Behaviour is mainly shown?

options.text: Making Effective Decisions
Delivering at Pace
Working Together
Seeing the Big Picture

questions.hint: Resolving friction to keep a group working is Working Together.

items.title: L6: Reading the advert for Lead Behaviours
items.body: A Civil Service advert says which Success Profiles elements will be assessed and often which Behaviours will be tested at each stage. These are sometimes called lead Behaviours. A common pattern is that a short application or personal statement tests a small number of Behaviours, the sift decides who goes forward, and the interview tests those or more of the Behaviours, sometimes with Strengths questions as well. The advert also sets word limits, so you may be asked for a statement of around 250 words per Behaviour or a single statement of several hundred words covering two or three. Always check the advert, because departments differ. Read the Behaviours at the grade being advertised. The same Behaviour name is used at every grade, but the expectation rises: at AO level the focus is on your own work and immediate team, at EO level you are usually guiding others or coordinating work, and at HEO level you are usually leading a team or area and making choices that affect others. If an advert lists Delivering at Pace and Managing a Quality Service, your two stories should each be chosen for one of those, and each story should show you working at about the right scale for the grade. A story about running a household rota is fine for an AO role. For a HEO role, assessors would expect more, such as influencing people over whom you have no authority or balancing competing priorities.

questions.prompt: An advert lists three lead Behaviours and a 500-word statement. What is the sensible approach?

options.text: Choose a separate story for each Behaviour and split the words roughly evenly
Write one long story and mention all three Behaviours in the final paragraph so that every one is covered
Spend all 500 words on whichever Behaviour you find the easiest to write
Write about Strengths instead, because they carry more weight in the sift

questions.hint: Each Behaviour needs its own evidence within the limit.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the same Behaviour name appearing at different grades is correct?

options.text: The wording changes completely at each grade, so earlier examples never apply
The name stays the same but the expectation rises with the grade
Only the Technical element changes with grade
Higher grades are assessed on fewer Behaviours

questions.hint: The grade changes the level of the Behaviour, not its name.

questions.prompt: At which grade would an assessor usually expect you to be coordinating or guiding others in the evidence?

options.text: Administrative Assistant
Administrative Officer
Executive Officer
Any grade, since the expectation does not change

questions.hint: EO evidence usually shows guiding others.

questions.prompt: A HEO advert lists Working Together. Which example is the best match?

options.text: Helping a colleague who sits next to you to find a form quickly and then showing her where it is filed
Getting two teams with competing priorities to agree a shared plan
Following a rota that has been arranged by somebody else
Attending every team meeting on time and taking notes

questions.hint: HEO evidence usually involves influence beyond your own work.

questions.prompt: Where should you look first to find out which elements and Behaviours will be tested?

options.text: The advert and the candidate information attached to it
A general website that gives interview tips for any employer
Last year's advert for a different Civil Service department
The annual report published by the department you are applying to

questions.hint: Departments differ, so the advert itself is the guide.

questions.prompt: What does a sift usually do in the process?

options.text: Gives a final job offer to the highest-scoring applicant
Decides which applicants go forward to the next stage
Replaces the interview stage in every Civil Service recruitment
Checks only whether the application form is spelled correctly

questions.hint: The sift narrows the field.

questions.prompt: An advert asks for Delivering at Pace and Managing a Quality Service. How should you choose stories?

options.text: Two stories that both show Delivering at Pace, as the first listed is more important
One story that you hope covers both
Any two stories, since the Behaviour names are only labels
One story chosen for each Behaviour, each at about the right scale for the grade

questions.hint: Each listed Behaviour needs matching evidence.

questions.prompt: For an AO role, a candidate describes running a household rota. How would assessors usually view this?

options.text: It is not acceptable, because it was unpaid work done at home
It is acceptable evidence, because the scale suits AO level
It is too small to be worth mentioning in any application
It can only be used as Strengths evidence, not as a Behaviour

questions.hint: Home experience is valid at a suitable scale.

questions.prompt: A department's advert gives its own word limit that differs from a friend's earlier application. What should you do?

options.text: Use your friend's limit, because that application was successful and the same limit is likely to apply again
Ignore both limits and write as much as you need to
Follow the current advert, as limits vary between departments and campaigns
Write to the old limit and add the rest as an attachment

questions.hint: The advert in front of you governs.

questions.prompt: Why is it risky to prepare only for the Behaviours you expect at interview?

options.text: Interviews never cover the Behaviours that were listed in the advert, because those are only used for the sift
Assessors dislike candidates who have prepared their answers in advance
Only Strengths questions are ever asked at an interview
The panel may test other lead Behaviours or Strengths named in the advert

questions.hint: Preparation should cover everything the advert names.

items.title: L6: Seeing the Big Picture and Making Effective Decisions
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Seeing the Big Picture and Making Effective Decisions are easily confused because both involve thinking beyond the task in front of you. The difference is the purpose. Seeing the Big Picture is about understanding how your work fits the aims of your team, your department and the public it serves, and letting that understanding guide how you work. Making Effective Decisions is about weighing information, options and risks, reaching a sensible choice and being able to explain it. A person showing Seeing the Big Picture might notice that a delay in her team's letters pushes more calls onto the helpline, and so decide to prioritise letters that trigger payments. A person showing Making Effective Decisions might compare two ways to clear the backlog, check the figures for each, consult a more experienced colleague and choose the one with fewer risks. Good decision evidence includes the information used, the options considered, the reason for the choice and what happened. It also shows judgement about when to decide alone and when to escalate. For example, an entry-level officer may decide how to order her own work but should refer a request outside her authority. Weak decision stories say 'I decided to' without any weighing. Weak Big Picture stories describe a task without any link to wider aims. In both cases the missing ingredient is usually the reason, so always say why.

questions.prompt: A processor notices that late letters push more calls onto the helpline, so she prioritises letters that trigger payments. Which Behaviour is mainly shown?

options.text: Making Effective Decisions
Seeing the Big Picture
Delivering at Pace
Managing a Quality Service

questions.hint: She links her work to wider effects and aims.

questions.prompt: A volunteer compares two ways to clear a backlog, checks the figures and takes advice before choosing one. Which Behaviour is mainly shown?

options.text: Seeing the Big Picture
Communicating and Influencing
Making Effective Decisions
Leadership

questions.hint: The story centres on weighing options and reaching a choice.

questions.prompt: Which ingredient is most often missing from a weak Making Effective Decisions answer?

options.text: The department's name and the team the person worked in
A description of the office layout and the tools used
The weighing of options and the reason for the choice
The exact date on which the decision was taken

questions.hint: Strong decision evidence shows how and why.

questions.prompt: What does Seeing the Big Picture require that a task description alone does not show?

options.text: A detailed list of the tools and systems that were used in the work, with the dates they were introduced
A link between the work and the aims of the team, department or public
The names and job titles of the other people involved
A much longer description of the task itself

questions.hint: The link to wider aims is the Behaviour.

questions.prompt: An officer is asked by a customer for something outside her authority. Which action best shows good decision-making?

options.text: Explain what she cannot do and refer the request to the right person
Grant it, to avoid the risk of a complaint being made
Ignore the request and carry on with her queue of work
Invent a rule that sounds plausible and apply it, so that the customer is not left without an answer

questions.hint: Knowing when to escalate is part of sound judgement.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is the better evidence of Making Effective Decisions?

options.text: 'I decided what to do, and in the end it worked out well for everyone.'
'I am a decisive person who is able to make quick choices under pressure.'
'The team decided to carry on exactly as it had before the problem arose, and I went along with that for the sake of the group.'
'I weighed up the cost of each option, asked a colleague and chose the cheaper, lower-risk one.'

questions.hint: A reason and an alternative make the decision visible.

questions.prompt: A person says 'I always check the figures because they matter to the department'. Which Behaviour is she hinting at, and what is missing?

options.text: Delivering at Pace, but she needs a date and a deadline
Seeing the Big Picture, but she needs a specific example of when it changed her work
Leadership, but she needs to name a team she managed
Communicating and Influencing, but she needs a quote from a colleague who saw her work and can confirm the change

questions.hint: A general claim needs a concrete example.

questions.prompt: Which of these is the best Result for a decision story?

options.text: The outcome of the choice and what she would check differently next time
A statement saying that the decision she took was a brave one and that she would take it again
A comment that nobody complained about what she had done
A reminder of the options she had rejected before choosing

questions.hint: Results should show outcome and learning.

questions.prompt: When is it reasonable to take a decision alone at entry level?

options.text: When it concerns the order or method of your own work, within agreed rules
When it affects whether a customer is entitled to a payment, since she knows the case best and can decide quickly
When the policy is unclear but you have a suspicion of the answer
When your manager is busy and the customer wants an answer today

questions.hint: Own-work choices are yours; entitlements are not.

questions.prompt: Which of these shows seeing the bigger picture rather than only completing a task?

options.text: Dealing with the cases strictly in the order they arrived, without question
Prioritising the cases that affect the most people waiting for payment
Copying the way a colleague sorts the post each morning
Working through lunch each day so that she can finish early

questions.hint: Prioritising by impact reflects wider aims.

items.title: L6: Communicating and Influencing or Working Together?
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Communicating and Influencing and Working Together both involve other people, so candidates often use the wrong one. Communicating and Influencing is about the message: choosing the right words and format for the audience, listening, explaining clearly, and persuading someone to see a point or act. The success test is whether the other person understood or was persuaded. Working Together is about the relationship and the shared goal: building trust, supporting colleagues, sharing information and resolving differences so that the group achieves more. The success test is whether the group worked better. A person who rewrites a confusing leaflet in plain English and checks it with three customers is showing Communicating and Influencing. A person who covers a colleague's duties during a difficult week, and agrees a handover so nothing is missed, is showing Working Together. Some stories show both. A volunteer who persuades a reluctant helper to join a team by listening to her worries shows influencing, but if the main effect is a cooperating team, Working Together leads. To decide, ask what changed: did someone's understanding or mind change, or did the way people cooperated change? Strong answers say who the other people were, what they needed, and what the candidate did differently for them. Phrases like 'I got on with everyone' are weak because they describe a feeling rather than an action.

questions.prompt: A volunteer rewrites a confusing leaflet in plain English and tests it with three customers. Which Behaviour is mainly shown?

options.text: Working Together
Changing and Improving
Communicating and Influencing
Delivering at Pace

questions.hint: The story is about getting a clear message across.

questions.prompt: An officer covers a colleague's duties during a hard week and agrees a handover so nothing is missed. Which Behaviour is mainly shown?

options.text: Communicating and Influencing
Working Together
Leadership
Managing a Quality Service

questions.hint: The story is about supporting colleagues to meet a shared goal.

questions.prompt: What is the simplest question for choosing between the two Behaviours?

options.text: Which of the two Behaviour names has the longer title or the more detailed description in the advert?
Was the other person involved more senior than I was at the time?
Did someone's understanding change, or did the way people cooperate change?
Did the event happen inside work, or somewhere outside work?

questions.hint: Message versus relationship separates the two.

questions.prompt: A volunteer persuades a reluctant helper to join by listening to her worries. The result is a team that now cooperates well. Which Behaviour should lead?

options.text: Communicating and Influencing, because she persuaded one person
Leadership, because she recruited a new helper to the group
Developing Self and Others, because the helper then learned the routine
Working Together, because the main effect is a cooperating team

questions.hint: The outcome decided the lead Behaviour.

questions.prompt: Which is the weakest evidence of Working Together?

options.text: 'I shared my notes with the new starter and agreed a weekly catch-up.'
'I asked the other team what they needed before the deadline.'
'I get on well with everyone.'
'I took on two of her cases when she was off sick.'

questions.hint: It describes a feeling, not an action.

questions.prompt: Which action best shows influencing rather than instructing?

options.text: Listening to a colleague's concerns and using them to explain how a change helps her
Telling her the change is compulsory and the date it starts
Sending an identical email about the change to everyone in the office, so that everybody gets exactly the same information
Asking her manager to talk to her about the change instead

questions.hint: Influencing works with the other person's needs.

questions.prompt: A candidate describes a presentation to a hall of parents but never says how it was received. What is missing?

options.text: The name of the school or hall where the event was held
The title and design of the presentation slides used
The time the event started and finished, and the number of seats that were set out in the hall
Evidence the message landed, such as questions asked or action taken

questions.hint: Communication evidence needs a response.

questions.prompt: Which audience adaptation is the best example of Communicating and Influencing?

options.text: Using a phone call rather than an email for a customer who struggles to read
Sending every message in the same standard format for consistency, so that nobody receives different treatment
Using technical terms in each message to sound more professional
Copying every message to a manager for the record

questions.hint: Matching method to the audience is key.

questions.prompt: Which phrase most clearly signals Working Together?

options.text: 'I spoke clearly and confidently when I addressed the whole group, and people could hear every word I said.'
'I wrote the report in plain language so that it could be understood.'
'I agreed with the other team how we would split the checks so neither of us duplicated work.'
'I made the final decision about who would do each task.'

questions.hint: Shared planning is cooperation.

questions.prompt: Why is a story with several people and no clear role for the candidate weak for either Behaviour?

options.text: Group stories are not allowed in Civil Service applications
The story would be too long to fit in the word limit once every person involved had been described
Assessors cannot tell what the candidate personally contributed
It would make the candidate seem more senior than she was

questions.hint: The Behaviour must be what the candidate did.

items.title: L6: Changing and Improving or Managing a Quality Service?
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Changing and Improving is about doing things differently and better: spotting a problem or opportunity, suggesting or trying a new approach, and seeing it through. Managing a Quality Service is about delivering a reliable, accurate, customer-focused service, following procedures, checking your work and putting things right when they go wrong. One looks forward to something new, the other protects a standard. A clerk who notices that customers keep asking the same question and drafts a clear information sheet is showing Changing and Improving. A clerk who double-checks every payment against the source record, corrects a mistake before it reaches the customer and records what happened is showing Managing a Quality Service. Be careful with the middle ground. A candidate who fixes an error is not necessarily improving the process unless they also changed how the work is done to prevent a repeat. The word 'improve' alone is not evidence. Good Changing and Improving evidence includes what was wrong, what was tried, who agreed to it, and the measurable difference afterwards. Good Managing a Quality Service evidence includes the standard, how it was checked, what went wrong and what was done for the customer. Remember that entry-level roles usually expect you to suggest improvements rather than to redesign whole processes, and that following a procedure carefully is a strength, not a lack of initiative.

questions.prompt: A clerk notices customers keep asking the same question and drafts an information sheet. Which Behaviour is mainly shown?

options.text: Managing a Quality Service
Changing and Improving
Delivering at Pace
Leadership

questions.hint: A new way of working to prevent repeated queries is improvement.

questions.prompt: A clerk checks each payment against the source record, corrects an error before it reaches the customer and logs what happened. Which Behaviour is mainly shown?

options.text: Managing a Quality Service
Changing and Improving
Seeing the Big Picture
Working Together

questions.hint: Accuracy, checking and correction protect the standard.

questions.prompt: A candidate fixes a recurring error each week but never changes the cause. Which statement is fair?

options.text: It is strong evidence of Changing and Improving because errors were found
It shows no Behaviour at all
It shows quality work, but is weak evidence of Changing and Improving
It is strong Leadership evidence

questions.hint: Fixing is not the same as preventing.

questions.prompt: Which detail is most important in a Changing and Improving answer?

options.text: What was tried, who agreed to it, and the difference it made afterwards
The number of colleagues who work in the same office and how long each of them has been in the post
A description of the software that the team uses
How long the candidate had been in the post

questions.hint: Improvement needs a before and after.

questions.prompt: At entry level, what is usually expected under Changing and Improving?

options.text: Redesigning a whole process for the department on your own, from the first draft to the final rollout
Suggesting and trying small improvements within your own work
Announcing a new policy to the rest of the team
Keeping to procedures and avoiding any change at all

questions.hint: Scale matches the grade.

questions.prompt: Which statement about following procedures is most accurate?

options.text: Following a procedure carefully is a strength under Managing a Quality Service
Following a procedure shows a lack of initiative, so it should be left out of a strong application altogether
Following procedures only matters at the more senior grades
Following a procedure is evidence of Changing and Improving

questions.hint: Reliable adherence protects the service.

questions.prompt: A shop assistant notices that price labels often fall off, tries a different type of sticker and tells her manager the results. Which Behaviour is mainly shown?

options.text: Managing a Quality Service
Communicating and Influencing
Changing and Improving
Working Together

questions.hint: She tried something new and reported the effect.

questions.prompt: Which is the best Result for a Managing a Quality Service answer?

options.text: The candidate felt proud of the accuracy of their work
The department went on to win a service award that year because of the way the candidate handled the error
The candidate was promoted shortly after the error was found
The customer got the correct amount and the error was recorded for tracking

questions.hint: Result shows the customer outcome and follow-up.

questions.prompt: Why is 'I improved the filing system' weak evidence?

options.text: Filing is not regarded as a work skill in the Civil Service, so it should not be described as an improvement
It does not say what was wrong, what changed or what difference it made
Improvements must always involve a new piece of technology
Only managers are able to improve a system or process

questions.hint: Specifics make the improvement visible.

questions.prompt: Which sentence best separates the two Behaviours?

options.text: One is meant for managers and the other is meant for new starters, so they are used at different grades
One is about speed of delivery; the other is about people
One protects a service standard; the other finds a better way of working
They are two names for exactly the same Behaviour

questions.hint: The first protects, the second renews.

items.title: L6: Delivering at Pace without losing accuracy
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Delivering at Pace is about taking responsibility for achieving results, planning and prioritising, and keeping work moving in line with deadlines. The most common mistake is to describe working fast and leaving out the planning. The second mistake is to confuse pace with Managing a Quality Service. A person who spends an extra hour checking every record is showing quality, not pace, unless the story is about how they kept a deadline while doing it. Strong pace evidence includes a deadline or volume, the competing demands, how the person prioritised, what they did to keep on track and the outcome. For example, an officer with 200 forms due by Friday might sort them by urgency, set a daily target, ask for help with one batch when she was behind, and finish a day early. Notice that asking for help is a good sign of judgement, not a weakness. Equally, rushing is not pace. If the officer had skipped checks to hit the date and created errors, the story would be a poor example. Sensible candidates also show resilience: what they did when plans changed. A realistic pace story includes a problem. For example, a colleague went off sick and priorities shifted, so the officer replanned the week. Without a problem, there is nothing for assessors to judge.

questions.prompt: An officer has 200 forms due by Friday, sorts them by urgency, sets a daily target and asks for help with one batch when behind. Which Behaviour is mainly shown?

options.text: Managing a Quality Service
Seeing the Big Picture
Developing Self and Others
Delivering at Pace

questions.hint: Planning and prioritising to a deadline is pace.

questions.prompt: What is the most common mistake in a Delivering at Pace answer?

options.text: Using too many numbers when describing the deadline, so that the story reads like a list of figures
Describing hard work or speed with no planning or prioritising
Mentioning a deadline at all in the opening Situation
Describing a problem that came up during the work

questions.hint: Planning is the visible part of pace.

questions.prompt: The officer asked for help with one batch when she was behind. How should this be seen?

options.text: As sound judgement that helped meet the deadline
As a sign that she could not cope with the role and had not planned her workload properly
As irrelevant to Delivering at Pace
As poor teamwork

questions.hint: Asking early is good judgement.

questions.prompt: A candidate skipped checks to meet a deadline and created errors. Why is the story a poor example of Delivering at Pace?

options.text: Meeting a deadline is never evidence
The errors were minor
Deadlines are not part of the Behaviour, which is about the quality of what is delivered
Rushing that reduces quality is not good delivery

questions.hint: Pace should not damage the standard.

questions.prompt: Which story is better evidence of Delivering at Pace than Managing a Quality Service?

options.text: Spending an extra hour verifying each record before it was released to the customer and logging the check each time
Writing a procedure for double-checking every single entry
Phoning customers to confirm that their details were correct
Reorganising a week's work after a colleague went off sick, so a deadline was met

questions.hint: The planning to meet a date is pace.

questions.prompt: Why should a pace story include a problem or change of plan?

options.text: Stories without a problem are not accepted by the sift panel
It makes the answer longer and helps it reach the word limit
Problems are the only way of showing that a deadline existed, so a pace story must always include one
It gives assessors something to judge about how you responded

questions.hint: Judgement shows in the response.

questions.prompt: Which phrase is the strongest evidence of prioritising?

options.text: 'I worked through the pile as fast as I possibly could.'
'I always put in extra effort when the pressure is on.'
'I ranked the cases by payment date and did those due soonest first.'
'I did everything that was on my list by the end of the day, so no work was carried over to the next one.'

questions.hint: A basis for ordering shows prioritisation.

questions.prompt: What should the Result of a pace answer state?

options.text: How tired the candidate was by the end and how many hours of overtime were worked
What was delivered, by when, and what the effect was
Which tool was used
How many people watched

questions.hint: Outcome and timing matter.

questions.prompt: A volunteer arranges transport for a trip, but three drivers drop out two days before. What would be the best evidence of Delivering at Pace?

options.text: Finding other drivers, re-planning pick-ups and confirming everyone on time
Cancelling the trip and telling the passengers to try again another time when more drivers are available
Telling the organiser that the late changes were not her fault
Waiting to see whether the drivers would come back

questions.hint: Adapting plans to keep to the deadline.

questions.prompt: How does 'I always meet deadlines' compare with a specific story?

options.text: It is stronger, because it is confident, short and shows that the candidate takes deadlines seriously
It is equal to a story, since both show reliability
It is a general claim and scores lower than a specific example
It is acceptable only for the most senior grades

questions.hint: Evidence beats assertion.

items.title: L6: Developing Self and Others in practice
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Developing Self and Others has two halves, and a good answer usually leans on one of them. Developing yourself means taking responsibility for your own learning: asking for feedback, identifying a gap, acting on it, and applying what you learned. Developing others means helping colleagues to learn, for example by showing a task, giving useful feedback or sharing knowledge. At entry level, evidence of developing yourself is expected, and helping others is often a welcome bonus. At higher grades the balance moves toward developing others and building the capability of a team. Suppose a new officer finds she makes mistakes in a complex form. She asks an experienced colleague to watch her complete one, writes herself a checklist from the feedback and uses it for two weeks, and her errors fall from several a week to one. That is strong self-development evidence because it has a gap, a response and a measured result. A common weakness is describing a training course without saying what changed afterwards. Attending a course is an input; applying the learning is the evidence. Another weakness is describing teaching in vague terms such as 'I trained the new person'. A better description says what she taught, how she checked understanding and how well the person then performed. Accepting feedback calmly, rather than defending yourself, is also part of the Behaviour.

questions.prompt: A new officer asks a colleague to watch her complete a form, writes a checklist from the feedback and sees her errors fall. Which Behaviour is mainly shown?

options.text: Managing a Quality Service
Changing and Improving
Developing Self and Others
Working Together

questions.hint: She identified a gap and acted on feedback to improve.

questions.prompt: What is the main weakness of 'I attended a three-day course on customer service'?

options.text: Courses are not accepted as evidence
It does not say what changed afterwards
It should have been four days
It is too long for a Result and takes up words that are needed elsewhere

questions.hint: Applying the learning is the evidence.

questions.prompt: At entry level, which is usually expected to be evidenced under Developing Self and Others?

options.text: Taking responsibility for your own learning
Managing the careers and development plans of other members of staff
Designing a training programme
Appraising colleagues

questions.hint: Self-development is the baseline.

questions.prompt: Which description of helping a new starter is strongest?

options.text: 'I showed her each step, watched her do one, corrected two slips and she did the next ten alone.'
'I trained the new person in how we do things here.'
'I am good at teaching other people new tasks, and colleagues often say that I explain things well.'
'I was there whenever she needed to ask me something.'

questions.hint: Specific teaching and a measured outcome score better.

questions.prompt: How should a candidate describe receiving criticism of her work to show the Behaviour?

options.text: Saying she disagreed but kept quiet to avoid a row, then carrying on exactly as before
Saying she had not needed the feedback in the first place
Listening, asking questions, changing what she did and checking it worked
Passing the comments on to a colleague to deal with

questions.hint: The Behaviour includes acting on feedback.

questions.prompt: As grades rise, how does the balance in Developing Self and Others usually shift?

options.text: Towards developing others and building the capability of a team
Away from learning of any kind and towards pure task delivery and the meeting of targets
Towards technical skill only, with no people element
Towards training external suppliers and partners

questions.hint: Leaders are expected to grow others.

questions.prompt: Which pair of ideas best sums up the Behaviour?

options.text: Winning arguments and avoiding errors in your work
Learning for yourself and helping others to learn
Delivering quickly and keeping costs down
Reporting results and keeping accurate records

questions.hint: Both halves are named in the Behaviour.

questions.prompt: Why does a measured result matter in a self-development story?

options.text: It makes the story longer and helps fill the word limit
It shows the learning was applied and made a difference
Assessors score only the answers that contain numbers
It shows that she did all of the work alone

questions.hint: Application and impact are the evidence.

questions.prompt: A volunteer coaches a younger helper to run the till but never checks whether she understood. What is the gap in the evidence?

options.text: Whether she understood, and what the coaching achieved, is never shown
The till is never mentioned
The helper's age and how long she had been volunteering are not given
The shop and its customers are not described

questions.hint: Developing others needs an outcome.

questions.prompt: Which situation shows a gap identified and acted on?

options.text: 'I sometimes find spreadsheets hard to use, so I ask other people to do that part of the work for me.'
'I would like to learn more about them one day.'
'My manager told me that I should go on a course.'
'My spreadsheet skills held me back, so I took a short online course and rebuilt the monthly report in half the time.'

questions.hint: Gap, action and result.

items.title: L6: Leadership at entry level
items.source: Civil Service Code and Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Leadership at AO and EO level does not mean managing people. In the Behaviours, it is about showing pride and passion for public service, being positive about change, being honest and respectful, and setting a good example. The Civil Service Code sets out the core values of integrity, honesty, objectivity and impartiality, and these underpin how a leader at any grade acts. At entry level, the evidence is usually about personal example. A person who notices that a newcomer is struggling and takes time to explain the routine is showing leadership, as is a person who tells a manager about a mistake she made, rather than hiding it. Equally, a person who stays positive when a new system is introduced and helps colleagues use it is showing leadership by example. At EO level, expect to lead by example and begin to guide small pieces of work, for example coordinating a rota or steering a short project. At HEO level the expectation is of managing a team, setting direction and handling performance. Weak Leadership answers claim titles. 'I was team leader at the shop' tells assessors nothing without what the person did. A better approach is to describe a moment where you took initiative, influenced others by your behaviour or took responsibility for an outcome. Honesty about errors is often the strongest evidence of integrity.

questions.prompt: What does Leadership usually mean at AO level?

options.text: Setting a good example, being positive and respectful, and being honest
Managing a team of staff, handling their performance and approving their leave and training
Setting the direction and strategy for the whole department
Signing off budgets and approving spending for the team

questions.hint: Entry-level leadership is about personal example.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a Civil Service Code core value?

options.text: Efficiency
Profit
Competitiveness
Impartiality

questions.hint: Integrity, honesty, objectivity and impartiality are the values.

questions.prompt: A clerk tells her manager about a mistake she made instead of hiding it. Which Behaviour is mainly shown?

options.text: Leadership
Delivering at Pace
Changing and Improving
Seeing the Big Picture

questions.hint: Honesty and personal example are leadership.

questions.prompt: Why is 'I was team leader at the shop' a weak answer?

options.text: Shop experience is not accepted for Civil Service jobs, so it cannot be used as evidence
Job titles can never be mentioned in an application
It is too short to be read by the assessor
It claims a title without saying what the candidate actually did

questions.hint: Behaviours need actions.

questions.prompt: An employee stays positive when a new system arrives and helps colleagues use it. Which Behaviour is mainly shown?

options.text: Leadership
Managing a Quality Service
Delivering at Pace
Making Effective Decisions

questions.hint: Positive example during change.

questions.prompt: At EO level, what might a Leadership example reasonably include?

options.text: Coordinating a rota or steering a short piece of work
Directing the work of a whole directorate
Setting the pay and grading of other staff
Leaving every decision about the work to the line manager, to avoid mistakes

questions.hint: EO evidence is often guiding small pieces of work.

questions.prompt: Which action best shows integrity?

options.text: Quietly correcting the error and saying nothing about it to anybody, since the customer has been paid
Blaming a colleague for the mistake in the decision
Reporting an error in a decision that favoured a customer
Waiting to see if anybody else notices the error

questions.hint: Openness about mistakes is integrity.

questions.prompt: Which story is the best Leadership evidence for an EO application?

options.text: Attending every team meeting on time and taking careful notes for people who were absent
Signing the attendance register each morning on arrival
Taking over a rota when its organiser left and checking colleagues coped
Having a long record of service in the same team

questions.hint: Taking responsibility and supporting colleagues is leadership.

questions.prompt: Which description is weakest as evidence of Leadership?

options.text: 'I explained the routine to a newcomer and checked she was comfortable.'
'I admitted the error and corrected it the same day.'
'I am a natural leader and people follow me.'
'I volunteered to try the new system first and shared tips.'

questions.hint: A claim without an action is weak.

questions.prompt: How does HEO-level Leadership differ most from AO-level?

options.text: It involves managing a team, setting direction and handling performance
It no longer involves honesty or integrity in any form
It no longer involves honesty or integrity, because those are expected only at entry level
It requires specific technical qualifications to be held

questions.hint: Responsibility for others rises with grade.

items.title: L6: Strong Results in STAR answers
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: The Result is the part of a STAR answer that candidates most often shorten or skip, yet assessors rely on it to judge whether the Action worked. A strong Result has three parts: the outcome, the evidence for it, and the learning or follow-up. The outcome says what changed for the customer, team or service. The evidence is a number, a comment or an observable change, such as 'the queue at 9am fell from about thirty to about ten' or 'the supervisor asked me to show the method to the rest of the team'. The learning shows reflection, such as what you would repeat or change. Do not exaggerate: if you do not know the exact figure, say 'roughly' or describe what you observed. A Result can also be honest about partial success. 'We reduced the errors by half but did not remove them, so I added a second check' can score as well as a perfect outcome, because it shows realism. Avoid results that are only feelings ('I felt proud') or generalities ('it went well'). Also avoid results that reward the team without naming your part, because assessors need to see what happened as a consequence of what you did. Remember that every number must be one you could explain at interview if asked how you arrived at it. If the result is unmeasured, use a comment, a repeated request or a change in behaviour.

questions.prompt: Which is the strongest Result?

options.text: 'It went really well, and everybody involved was happy with how everything turned out in the end.'
'I felt very proud of what I had managed to achieve.'
'We did a good job as a team and the work got done.'
'Returned post fell from about thirty items a week to ten, and my supervisor asked me to show the team.'

questions.hint: Specific outcome with evidence.

questions.prompt: What are the three parts of a strong Result?

options.text: The date, the place and the names of everybody who took part in the events described
The outcome, the evidence for it, and the learning or follow-up
The task, the action and the situation described in order
The apology, the thanks and the closing remark

questions.hint: These three parts make a Result convincing.

questions.prompt: What should a candidate do if she cannot recall the exact figure?

options.text: Choose a convincing number that is probably close, so that the Result still sounds strong
Leave the Result out
Use the department's average
Say 'roughly' or describe what she observed

questions.hint: Honesty beats invented precision.

questions.prompt: 'We reduced errors by half but did not remove them, so I added a second check.' How would this Result be viewed?

options.text: Realistic and strong, because it shows judgement and follow-up
Weak, because the problem was not solved completely and a Result should always be a full success
Dishonest, because it admits that something did not work
Irrelevant, because it is about errors and not a Behaviour

questions.hint: Honest partial success with follow-up scores well.

questions.prompt: Why is 'I felt proud' a poor Result?

options.text: Feelings are not allowed in applications, so any mention of pride is automatically marked down
It is too short
It describes a feeling, not an effect on the service
It uses the word I

questions.hint: Assessors need outcomes.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with a Result that credits only 'the team'?

options.text: It does not show what happened as a result of the candidate's own actions
Teams cannot achieve results without a named leader
It makes the answer too long for the word limit
It fails to include a deadline for the work or a date by which the outcome was seen

questions.hint: Assessors score the candidate's contribution.

questions.prompt: If a result cannot be measured, which is the best alternative evidence?

options.text: A general statement that the work went well on the whole and the customer seemed satisfied
A specific comment, a repeated request or an observable change in behaviour
A longer Action section to make up for the missing result
A promise to give more detail at the interview

questions.hint: Qualitative evidence can still be concrete.

questions.prompt: Which statement shows the learning part of a Result?

options.text: 'The event went to plan from beginning to end, and everything that we had arranged took place.'
'There were forty guests who attended on the day.'
'I would do it again in exactly the same way.'
'Next time I would check the supplier is available before promising a date.'

questions.hint: Reflection shows insight.

questions.prompt: A candidate gives a number in the Result. What should they be able to do at interview?

options.text: Prove it with a certificate
Cite a statistic from an official report
Explain how the number was arrived at
Show the interviewers a spreadsheet

questions.hint: Panels may probe the basis of figures.

questions.prompt: Which Result is least convincing?

options.text: 'The waiting list for the group dropped from twelve to four within a month.'
'The customer wrote to thank me for resolving it the same day.'
'It all worked out fine in the end.'
'My manager adopted the checklist for the whole team.'

questions.hint: It has no outcome or evidence.

items.title: L6: Writing strong Actions
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: The Action is the heart of a STAR answer and usually deserves around half of the words. It must show what you personally did, in a sensible order, and why. Three habits improve almost every Action. First, write 'I' for your own steps and use 'we' only for what the group did, so assessors can see your part. Second, use specific verbs: 'checked', 'drafted', 'asked', 'sorted', 'agreed' tell the reader more than 'dealt with', 'handled' or 'was involved in'. Third, include the reason for key steps, because reasoning is how judgement is shown. For example, 'I phoned the customer rather than emailing because she had told me she could not read small print' is much stronger than 'I contacted the customer'. Keep the steps in the order they happened so the story is easy to follow. Include any obstacle and what you did about it, because a smooth Action with no difficulty gives assessors little to score. Do not list everything. Pick three or four steps that best demonstrate the Behaviour being tested and cut the rest. Beware of the passive voice, such as 'the form was completed', which hides who did it, and of long preambles about the organisation, which use words without adding evidence. If the Behaviour is Communicating and Influencing, the Action should include how you adapted the message. If it is Delivering at Pace, it should include how you prioritised.

questions.prompt: Roughly how much of the words in a STAR answer should the Action usually take?

options.text: About five per cent
About a quarter
About ninety per cent
About half

questions.hint: The Action carries the evidence.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is the strongest Action?

options.text: 'I contacted the customer about the matter, and I made sure that she understood what we needed from her.'
'The customer was contacted about the problem.'
'We made sure the customer was reached in good time.'
'I phoned the customer rather than emailing, as she had said she could not read small print.'

questions.hint: A specific step with a reason.

questions.prompt: Why is 'the form was completed' a weak Action sentence?

options.text: It is too long
Forms are not relevant to the Behaviour, which is mainly about people
It is in the past tense
The passive voice hides who did the work

questions.hint: Assessors need to see the candidate's own actions.

questions.prompt: Which verb gives assessors the most information?

options.text: Dealt with
Handled
Drafted
Was involved in

questions.hint: Specific verbs show the actual step.

questions.prompt: Why should an Action include an obstacle?

options.text: It gives assessors judgement to score
Stories must have some drama, and an obstacle supplies it for the reader
It makes the Action shorter
Obstacles are required by the form

questions.hint: Overcoming difficulty reveals behaviours.

questions.prompt: A candidate lists twelve steps in a 250-word answer. What is the likely problem?

options.text: The steps are too few to show the Behaviour at all and need more padding with detail
The Result is given far too much space
The reasoning for each step is too detailed
Each step is thin and the key ones do not stand out

questions.hint: Choose the steps that best show the Behaviour.

questions.prompt: For a Communicating and Influencing answer, which element should the Action include?

options.text: How the candidate adapted the message for the audience
How quickly she typed the message and how many words per minute she managed
The layout of the room
The name of the software

questions.hint: The Behaviour is about the message and audience.

questions.prompt: Which is the best use of 'we' in an answer?

options.text: In every sentence, because it sounds modest and shows that she values the team
For what the group did, with 'I' for the candidate's own steps
Never, even for group actions
Only at the start

questions.hint: Clarity about your own role.

questions.prompt: Which opening wastes the most words?

options.text: 'The task was to cover reception on my own for a week.'
'Two helpers had dropped out of the event on the Friday.'
A long paragraph about the history and size of the organisation
'I had 200 forms that were due in by Friday, and my manager was on leave that week.'

questions.hint: Context should be brief.

questions.prompt: Why do the steps need to be in the order they happened?

options.text: So the story is chronological, because the application form is scored in the order of events
So the story is easy to follow and the reasoning is clear
So the Result comes first
Because order is scored separately

questions.hint: Sequence helps assessors follow the logic.

items.title: L6: Answering strengths questions well
items.body: Strengths-based questions are designed to find out what energises you, rather than what you can recite from experience. They are usually asked quickly, often in a series, and the interviewer watches for how you respond as much as what you say. Typical examples are 'What do you enjoy about helping people?' or 'Are you more of a planner or a go-with-the-flow person?'. Because there is no single right answer, the best approach is to be honest and specific, and to link your answer to the kind of work in the role. A strong strengths answer is short, natural and shows energy, such as 'I like it when a messy list becomes a clear plan, so I enjoy setting up the spreadsheet at the start of a project'. Unlike Behaviour questions, you do not need a full STAR structure, and a long rehearsed story can sound unnatural. Do not claim to love everything, because panels read this as insincere. Also, do not give an answer you think the panel wants if it is not true, since you will struggle to keep it up through a series of follow-up questions. Good preparation is to reflect on your own strengths and weaknesses using examples from home, study, volunteering and work, then read the advert to see which strengths match. During the interview, listen for the exact question, and answer it directly, with a short reason or example.

questions.prompt: What is a strengths-based question mainly designed to find out?

options.text: Which qualifications you hold
How many years of experience you have in the type of work advertised
How well you have memorised the Behaviours
What energises you and what you naturally do well

questions.hint: Strengths are about energy and natural talent.

questions.prompt: Which answer to 'Are you more of a planner or go-with-the-flow person?' is best?

options.text: 'I am a very good planner and I always have been, so I plan everything I do in great detail.'
'I never plan; I prefer to see what happens.'
'I can be both of those things at all times.'
'I plan the key points so I know what matters, then stay flexible when things change.'

questions.hint: A balanced honest answer with a reason.

questions.prompt: Why is a long rehearsed STAR story usually wrong for a strengths question?

options.text: STAR is meant only for written applications, so using it at interview counts against you
The panel dislikes stories
It takes longer than the interview slot
It can sound unnatural, and strengths questions are meant to be quick and spontaneous

questions.hint: Brief, natural answers fit the style.

questions.prompt: Why is 'I love every part of the job' a weak answer?

options.text: Enthusiasm lowers scores, because panels prefer a calm and neutral tone of voice
Panels read blanket enthusiasm as insincere
It is too short
It uses first person

questions.hint: Specific energy is more believable.

questions.prompt: Why is it unwise to answer with what you think the panel wants if it is untrue?

options.text: Panels never check
Follow-up questions will make the mismatch obvious
It breaks the Civil Service Code, which forbids saying anything that is not literally true
It makes the interview shorter

questions.hint: Authenticity is easier to sustain.

questions.prompt: How should you prepare for strengths questions?

options.text: Learn the names of all the Behaviours word for word
Reflect on what you enjoy and do well, using examples from home, study, volunteering and work
Write a script for every strengths question you can think of and learn each one word for word
Ask the panel in advance which questions they will use

questions.hint: Self-knowledge is the preparation.

questions.prompt: Which answer shows energy and a link to the role?

options.text: 'I am good at making lists, and I find that I can usually keep track of a large amount of work.'
'I have used spreadsheets in a previous job.'
'I like it when a messy list becomes a clear plan, so I enjoy setting up the spreadsheet at the start.'
'Planning is an important part of any project.'

questions.hint: Specific, natural and tied to the work.

questions.prompt: What should you do before answering a strengths question?

options.text: Listen for exactly what is asked and answer it directly
Ask for a minute to write notes, so that the answer can be properly structured
Give a generic answer you used earlier
Wait until the panel prompts you

questions.hint: Direct answers show listening.

questions.prompt: Which statement about Behaviour and strengths questions is accurate?

options.text: Strengths questions are only ever asked of senior staff, whereas Behaviour questions are for everyone
Behaviour questions are never asked at interview in the Civil Service
The two types of question are exactly the same
Behaviour questions ask for past evidence; strengths questions ask about natural preferences

questions.hint: The two types test different things.

questions.prompt: Which is the best way to match your strengths to a role?

options.text: Memorise a list of strengths used in other departments
Read the advert and the role description to see which strengths fit the work
Pick strengths at random from a list and hope that some of them match the role
Avoid any strength not listed in the advert

questions.hint: The advert shows the kind of work and strengths needed.

items.title: L6: Home and unpaid experience as evidence
items.source: Civil Service Jobs guidance and Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: The Experience element and the Behaviours both accept evidence from outside paid work: caring for a relative, running a household, volunteering, studying, community groups and sport all count when they show what the advert asks for. The skill is in choosing the right example and describing it in work language. Start with the Behaviour in the question, then ask which unpaid activity gave you the best chance to show it. A carer who manages medication, appointments and communication with professionals has strong evidence for Managing a Quality Service and Communicating and Influencing. A parent who organises a school fundraiser has strong evidence for Delivering at Pace and Working Together. A volunteer who trains new helpers shows Developing Self and Others. Use the same STAR structure: a clear situation, your task, your action and the result. Do not apologise for the setting or say 'it was only at home'. State the facts: what you were responsible for, how many people it involved, the time pressure and what you achieved. Do not exaggerate the scale. Also protect other people's privacy: you can describe 'a relative with a long-term health condition' without naming them or giving medical details. Finally, unpaid examples work at entry level, but for higher grades the scale and complexity expected increase, so an example that suits an AO application may need a bigger responsibility or wider influence for a HEO role.

questions.prompt: A carer manages medication, appointments and communication with professionals. Which two Behaviours does this most clearly support?

options.text: Leadership and Seeing the Big Picture
Changing and Improving and Delivering at Pace
Developing Self and Others and Working Together
Managing a Quality Service and Communicating and Influencing

questions.hint: Accuracy and liaison with professionals are the clearest links.

questions.prompt: A parent organises a school fundraiser. Which Behaviours does this best support?

options.text: Managing a Quality Service only, because the money has to be handled accurately
Making Effective Decisions only
Seeing the Big Picture only
Delivering at Pace and Working Together

questions.hint: Planning to a date with helpers.

questions.prompt: What is the first step when choosing a home or unpaid example?

options.text: Start with the Behaviour in the question and find the activity that best shows it
Pick the most recent activity you have done, whatever it was
Choose the activity that sounds the most impressive on paper, whether or not it matches the Behaviour
Select the activity you have done for the longest time

questions.hint: The Behaviour drives the choice.

questions.prompt: Why should you avoid saying 'it was only at home'?

options.text: Home examples are not accepted at all in applications, so any mention of them is a mistake
It uses up words that are needed for the Result
Assessors dislike candidates who sound modest
It undersells the evidence, and assessors judge what you did, not where

questions.hint: Setting does not decide quality.

questions.prompt: How should a candidate describe caring for a relative while protecting privacy?

options.text: As a relative with a long-term condition, without names or medical details
With full medical details, to prove the case is genuine
With the relative's name and address, so it can be checked
With the relative's name and address, so that the panel is able to check the facts for itself

questions.hint: Describe the responsibility, not the person's data.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the scale of unpaid examples is most accurate?

options.text: The scale is irrelevant at all grades
For higher grades, assessors expect larger responsibility or wider influence
Only the length of time matters
Higher grades use only paid examples, because unpaid work cannot reach the required scale

questions.hint: Expectation rises with grade.

questions.prompt: A volunteer trains new helpers to use the till and checks they cope. Which Behaviour does this best support?

options.text: Seeing the Big Picture
Delivering at Pace
Developing Self and Others
Making Effective Decisions

questions.hint: She is teaching others and checking understanding.

questions.prompt: Which sentence translates home experience into work language best?

options.text: 'I ran a household budget across several accounts, set up standing orders and cut costs by checking suppliers each quarter.'
'I sort out the bills at home, and I am always careful to pay everything on time and keep the receipts safe every month.'
'I am good with money and I have never been in debt, and I am careful about what I spend each month on everything.'
'I am a very organised person in all areas.'

questions.hint: Specific responsibility and action.

questions.prompt: Which approach is wrong when using unpaid experience?

options.text: Describing responsibilities clearly
Giving the real number of people involved
Inflating the scale of a small activity
Stating the time pressure

questions.hint: Exaggeration is dishonest and probed.

questions.prompt: Why use the STAR structure for unpaid examples?

options.text: Unpaid work cannot be described any other way
It is only needed for volunteering and not for home or caring examples, which are shorter
It gives the same clear evidence as for paid work
It reduces the word count

questions.hint: STAR works for any setting.
